Intensity drives adaptation

Harder work has a place. The trick is knowing what needs to be harder, and when.

Training · practical guide · Updated 2026-11-24

The same hill, a different day

There is a hill you know well. You know where the road steepens, where it flattens briefly, and roughly how far you have to go before you can stop thinking about the climb. A few months ago you had to slow down halfway up. Now you walk it without much fuss. That is progress. The question is what you do with it.

Hard is not always the same thing

You could put more weight in your pack. You could keep the weight and walk a little faster, or climb the hill twice. All three make the outing harder, but they do not ask the same thing of you. If you struggle on steep ground, adding another five kilos on a flat road might not address the problem. If your shoulders give out before your legs, sprinting every hill may not be the answer either.

Make the work count

For endurance, sometimes the useful change is another half hour at a pace you can hold. For climbing, it might be four controlled uphill efforts, with enough time on the way down to do the next one properly. For strength, it might be a heavier squat in the gym, where you can put the weight down when the set is done. There is no prize for making all three harder on the same day.

The work after the work

A hard session is an invitation for your body to adapt, not a guarantee that it will. Food, sleep and the time between demanding sessions matter. If Saturday leaves you dragging yourself through Tuesday, perhaps Saturday was too much. Some weeks the best decision is to repeat the last one. A session you can build on is worth more than one you spend a fortnight recovering from.

Keep a little record

Write down the route, load, time and what it felt like. How did the last third compare with the first? How did your legs feel the following morning? Next time, change one thing. It will not always be obvious that you are getting fitter, but a few months of ordinary notes can show you what the mirror and the scale cannot.

Go back to the hill

The easy days still belong in the plan. They give you room to practise, enjoy the walk and come back ready for a harder one. Intensity drives certain adaptations; the quieter work builds the base that lets you use that intensity. The hill will still be there next week. You do not have to settle the argument with it today.

Try this on your own route

Pick a familiar climb that takes roughly two minutes. After an easy warm-up, walk up four times at a strong pace you can still control, with an easy walk down between efforts. Keep your pack as it was last week. If your fourth climb looks nothing like your first, do not add a fifth just to fill the page. A few weeks later, compare the same climb, the same pack and how you felt the morning after. The result may be a faster climb, but it may also be the same climb feeling less expensive.

Put it into practice

If a mountain event is your goal, the useful hard work may be controlled climbing rather than a heavier flat ruck. Explore the different load categories at Fan Dance mountain challenge.
